'''yieldance†''' (yēl′dans), ''n.'' [< ''yield'' + ''-anc'' The act of yielding, producing, submitting, conceding; submission; surrender.
{{smaller block|He . . . sues, not so much for the prophet’s ''yielda'' as for his own life. {{right|''Bp. Hall'', Ahaziah S}}}}

'''yielden†''', ''p. a.'' Same as ''yolden.''

'''yielder''' (yēl′dėr), ''n.'' [< ME. ''ȝeldere;'' < ''yield'' ''-er''<sup>1</sup>.] '''1†.''' One who pays; a debtor.—'''2.''' C who yields, permits, or suffers; one who s renders, submits, or gives in.
{{smaller block|<poem>''Doug.'' Yield thee as my prisoner.
''Blunt.'' I was not born a ''yielder'', thou proud Scot.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', 1 Hen. IV., v. 3.}}}}

'''yielding''' (yēl′ding), ''n.'' [< ME. ''ȝeldinge;'' ver n. of ''yield'', ''v.''] '''1†.''' Payment. ''Prompt. Pa'' p. 537.—'''2.''' Compliance; assent; surrende
{{smaller block|<poem>Immaculate and spotless is my mind;
That was not forced; that never was inclined
To accessary ''yieldings.'' ''Shak.'', Lucrece, l. 1</poem>
It lies in the bosom of a sweet wife to draw her husb from any loose imperfection . . . by her politic ''yield''
{{right|''Dekker and Webster'', Northward Ho, }}}}
'''3.''' A giving away under physical pressure settling.
{{smaller block|Faults in sleepers, irregular ''yieldings'' on bridges, and other imperfections, were definitely marked.
{{right|''Nature'', XLIII.}}}}

'''yielding''' (yēl′ding), ''p. a.'' Inclined or fit to yi in any sense of the word; especially, soft; c pliant; unresisting.

{{smaller block|Sir knyght, thow art take; ''yelde'' thow to me, for y haue don I-nough.
{{right|''Merlin'' (E. E. T. S.), iii. 46}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Thus ''yields'' the cedar to the axe’s edge.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', 3 Hen. VI., v. 2. 1}}}}
{{smaller block|Sometimes I stand desperately to my arms, like the foot when deserted by their horse; not in hope to overcome, but only to ''yield'' on more honourable terms.
{{right|''Dryden'', Essay on Dram. Poesy, De}}}}
'''3.''' To give way, in a moral sense, as to entreaty, argument, or a request; cease opposing; comply; consent; assent.
{{smaller block|<poem>Ne hadde I er now, my swete herte deere,
Ben ''yolde'', ywis I were now noght here.</poem>
{{right|''Chaucer'', Troilus, iii. 121}}}}
{{smaller block|But at last, vpon much intreatie, hee ''yeelded'' to let him go to the General.
{{right|''Hakluyt’s Voyages'', II. i. 2}}}}
{{smaller block|Guendolen the Daughter [of Corineus] ''yeelds'' to marry
{{right|''Milton'', Hist. Eng.,}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>No more, dear love, for at a touch I ''yield'':
Ask me no more.</poem>
{{right|''Tennyson'', Princess, vi. (song}}}}
'''4.''' To give place, as inferior in rank or excellence.
{{smaller block|Their mutton ''yields'' to ours, but their beef is excellent
{{right|''Swift'', Gulliver’s Travels, i.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Tell me first, in what more happy fields
The thistle springs, to which the lily ''yields''.</poem>
{{right|''Pope'', Spring, l.}}}}

'''yield''' (yēld), ''n.''   [Early mod. E. also ''yeeld''; < M. E. ''yeld'', ''ʒeld'', ''ʒielde'', ''ʒild'', < AS. ''geld'', ''gield'', ''gild'', payment, = OS. ''geld'' = OFries. ''jeld'' = OHG. MHG. ''gelt'', payment, money, G. ''geld'', money, = Icel. ''gjald'', payment, etc.; from the verb: see ''yield'', ''v.'', and cf. ''gild''<sup>2</sup>, ''gelt''<sup>2</sup>.]   '''1†.''' {{right|[p. 329}}}}
'''2.''' That which is yielded; the product or r turn of growth, cultivation, or care; also, th which is obtained by labor, as in mines or ma ufactories.
{{smaller block|<poem>He shall be like the fruitful tree, . . .
Which in due season constantly
A goodly ''yield'' of fruit doth bring. ''Bacon'', Ps</poem>

{{right|''E. C. Grenville Murray'', Round about France, p.}}}}
{{smaller block|The ''yield'' of the machine is the quantity of electric put in motion in each unit of time.
{{right|''Atkinson'', tr. of Mascart and Joubert, I. 1}}}}
'''3.''' The act of yielding or giving way, as unc pressure. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|After pointing out that the permanent elongation of a under longitudinal stress consists of a sliding combi with an increase of volume, the author showed that ''yield'' is caused by the limit of elastic resistance (''p'') pa lel to one particular direction in the bar (generally at to the axis) being less than along any other direction.

'''yoicks''' (yoiks), ''interj.''   [Cf. ''hoicks.'']   An old fox-hunting cry.

'''yoit''' (yoit), ''n.'' Same as ''yite. Montagu.''   [Local, British.]
